extra_misconceptions.fact: Incising or sucking a snakebite damages tissue and risks infection; keep the limb immobilized below heart level and evacuate.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cutting across snakebite fang marks and sucking out the venom stops toxin spread in the field.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Suffocating or heating a tick makes it regurgitate infectious fluids into the wound; pull it straight out with fine tweezers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Smothering an attached tick with petroleum jelly or heat forces it to back out safely on its own.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Intact blister skin forms a sterile barrier against bacteria, so leave small blisters unbroken and pad them with moleskin.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping every friction blister on the trail immediately relieves pressure and speeds skin healing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Altered mental status and hot skin signal heatstroke, a medical emergency requiring rapid external cooling and immediate EMS.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A runner who stops sweating and becomes confused on a hot course only needs shade and cold water.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should fine-tipped tweezers grasp an embedded tick so its mouthparts release cleanly without squeezing the body?
Which physical indicator distinguishes life-threatening heatstroke from heat exhaustion during a warm-weather course?
What specific details about a snakebite and its timing should a buddy record before evacuating a runner to medical care?
Why is it dangerous to bushwhack through dense brush on an off-trail leg without recognizing local poisonous plants?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Orienteering rewards route choice and map reading across unmarked terrain, where a slower, accurate navigator beats a lost sprinter.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Orienteering races are won by the fastest sprinter following a marked trail from start to finish.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cross-country courses require visiting controls in exact numerical order, whereas score events allow choosing points freely.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Competitors in a standard cross-country event may visit the numbered control flags in any sequence.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Traditional foot orienteering prohibits GPS navigation aids, requiring competitors to rely solely on a map and magnetic compass.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Handheld GPS receivers and smartphone mapping apps are standard navigation tools in foot orienteering.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every competitor must report to the finish table even when abandoning a course so organizers do not launch a search party.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A runner who retires early from an orienteering course can head straight to camp without checking in.

extra_socratic_questions: What sequence of map and compass actions allows a competitor to navigate between control points in unfamiliar terrain?
What rules distinguish a cross-country point-to-point orienteering event from a timed score orienteering competition?
What verification mechanism on a control punch or electronic finger stick proves a runner visited each marker in order?
Why must every runner know the safety bearing and course closure time before leaving the start triangle?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The magnetized needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field lines and points toward Magnetic North rather than geographic True North.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The red end of a magnetic compass needle points directly toward the geographic North Pole on a map.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Staring at the compass causes lateral drift and tripping hazards; sight a distant landmark on the bearing and walk to that point.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Walking while staring continuously down at the compass dial is the most accurate way to hold a bearing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The needle moves independently of the bezel and remains aligned with Magnetic North while you turn the housing to set degrees.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rotating the compass bezel changes the direction in which the magnetized needle points inside the capsule.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Large bubbles can pin or deflect the lightweight magnetic needle on uneven ground, causing inaccurate degree readings in the field.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A large air bubble inside the liquid-filled compass housing has no effect on taking accurate bearings.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position the baseplate direction-of-travel arrow while rotating the body to put red in the shed?
What functional difference separates the rotating azimuth housing dial from the magnetized needle suspended in liquid?
What intermediate landmark method keeps you on a degree bearing when trees block your direct line of sight?
What happens to the magnetic needle reading if you hold your baseplate compass next to a steel belt buckle or phone?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Contour V-shapes in a valley or stream drainage always point upstream toward higher elevation, opposite the flow of water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: V-shaped contour lines that cross a stream always point downstream in the direction of water flow.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Earth's magnetic poles shift over time, so navigators must check the map date and update declination on older USGS quadrangles.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Magnetic declination stays constant forever on a printed topographic map regardless of publication year.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Dedicated orienteering maps are printed with meridian lines already aligned to Magnetic North, eliminating declination math.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Orienteering maps and standard USGS topographic maps both require manual degree calculations for declination.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wide spacing between contour lines represents gentle or flat terrain, whereas tightly packed or touching contours show steep slopes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Widely spaced brown contour lines on a topographic map indicate a steep cliff or vertical rock face.

extra_socratic_questions: Which direction do V-shaped contour lines point when they cross a creek or drainage draw on a topographic map?
What visual difference on a topographic map separates an enclosed hilltop contour loop from a depression contour?
What paper-strip technique measures the true curved trail distance between two points against the map bar scale?
What lateral position error occurs over one kilometer if you ignore a 15-degree declination on a USGS quad map?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A standard orienteering pace is a double step counted each time the same foot hits the ground, keeping numbers smaller and easier.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: One pace in orienteering distance measurement equals a single step taken by either the left or right foot.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Slopes, mud, and undergrowth shorten stride length, requiring more double-step paces to cover 100 meters of horizontal map distance.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A Scout's 100-meter pace count measured on a flat paved track stays identical in steep or marshy woods.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Running lengthens your stride, so your running pace count for 100 meters is lower than your walking pace count over flat ground.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Running a 100-meter leg requires the exact same number of double-step paces as walking the same distance.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A pace course must be laid out with a surveyor's tape or verified 100-meter track so stride errors do not compound across legs.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Measuring a 100-meter calibration course by estimating steps from another Scout is accurate enough for events.

extra_socratic_questions: Why do orienteers count every time the same foot strikes the ground rather than counting every individual step?
What happens to your 100-meter pace count when you transition from walking on a flat track to running uphill?
What averaging method across multiple out-and-back runs on a 100-meter tape produces a reliable personal pace table?
Why is a calibrated pace count essential when navigating toward a subtle control in low-visibility forest terrain?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Column A shows the sequential control order, while Column B gives the unique identification code printed on the field marker flag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The number printed in Column B of a control description sheet matches the sequential order of the control.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Aiming off intentionally biases your bearing left or right of the target so you know which way to turn upon hitting the line feature.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Aiming off means sighting your compass directly at a point feature on a trail and hoping not to drift.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A catching feature is a large linear barrier located past the control that alerts a runner they have overshot the target zone.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A catching feature is a prominent landmark located right in front of the control that leads you into it.

extra_misconceptions.fact: IOF control descriptions use standardized pictorial symbols in columns so competitors speaking any language get identical clues.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: International control description sheets use written English sentences so only English speakers can read them.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a runner aim when using aiming off to hit a stream-junction control located along a linear trail?
What tactical role separates a collecting feature used on approach from a catching feature beyond the control?
Which columns on an IOF control description sheet specify the exact feature and the flag position on that feature?
Under what terrain condition does contour-lining around a steep spur save more energy than climbing straight over?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A post-event route map must trace the exact trails, contours, and errors you actually traveled so you can analyze time losses.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Drawing straight lines between control circles on your post-race map accurately represents the route you ran.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Scouting America Youth Protection rules require the buddy system, so Scouts complete requirement 7a in pairs or small groups.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Scouts must run completely alone in the woods to satisfy the three-event requirement for the Orienteering badge.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Steep climbs, marshes, and thick green vegetation slow runners down, making a longer trail or contour route faster overall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The shortest straight-line path drawn in purple between two controls is always the fastest route on the ground.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Effective post-race reports isolate navigation mistakes such as parallel errors, missed attack points, or poor exit bearings.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Blaming slow overall times on running speed alone is enough analysis for an orienteering post-event report.

extra_socratic_questions: When should you draw your actual route on the competition map so you do not forget detours or hesitation points?
What split-time evidence distinguishes a poor strategic route choice from a technical compass execution error?
What specific leg-by-leg notes in your post-event report reveal why a longer trail route beat a straight bushwhack?
What buddy-system roles keep two Scouts together on a cross-country course while sharing map and compass duties?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Orienteering tests navigation rather than hide-and-seek, so flags must be visible once a runner reaches the described feature.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Good orienteering control placement means hiding the orange-and-white flag inside bushes so runners must search.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Score courses assign higher point values to distant or technically difficult controls to create strategic route-planning tradeoffs.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: All 12 controls on a score orienteering course should receive the exact same point value regardless of distance.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Official cross-country course length is measured as the sum of straight-line distances from the start through each control to finish.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Course length for a 2,000-meter cross-country event is measured along the longest possible trail detour route.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Course planners must vet every control site in the field to confirm map accuracy, vegetation changes, and safe footing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Desktop map work alone is sufficient to finalize a master map and control description sheet before an event.

extra_socratic_questions: What field-vetting step ensures each control flag hangs on the exact feature shown on the master map?
What design goal separates assigning point values on a 12-control score course from ordering a 2,000-meter course?
What map scale calculation confirms your five-control cross-country course meets the 2,000-meter minimum length?
Why must a course planner avoid placing control legs that tempt runners to cross cliffs, deep water, or busy roads?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Staggering start times by one to three minutes prevents runners from following each other and preserves solo navigation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Starting all competitors in the same class at once speeds up course administration without affecting navigation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Finish officials must match each unique pin-punch pattern in the exact numbered box sequence against the master control card.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Counting the total number of pin holes on a control card is enough to verify that a runner completed a cross-country course.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every starter must check in at the finish table even when retiring early so officials do not launch an overdue-runner search.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Runners who abandon a course early due to fatigue or injury can return straight to camp without visiting the finish table.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Master maps belong 20 to 50 meters past the start line so route copying and planning occur on the competitor's running time.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing the master maps directly at the start line allows runners to copy control circles before their clock begins.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to course fairness if the starter releases two runners on the same course less than two minutes apart?
Under what condition does a finish official classify a runner's control card as Did Not Finish instead of a mispunch?
What calculation confirms a competitor's net elapsed time when reconciling the finish clock against the start list?
Why is it dangerous to close the finish table before matching every registration stub against returned control cards?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Measuring a map bearing with a baseplate compass uses the map's meridian lines as a protractor regardless of how the sheet lies.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A topographic map must be oriented to magnetic north before you can measure a protractor bearing between two map points.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Orienteers count double paces every time the same foot strikes the ground to halve the mental tally and reduce counting errors.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Counting every single footstep is more accurate than counting every second step when measuring distance over rough ground.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Aiming deliberately a few degrees left or right of the target guarantees you know which direction to turn upon hitting the stream.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Aiming dead center at a stream junction gives a beginner the fastest recovery if compass drift occurs in thick woods.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Folding the map small and pinning your thumb on your current position keeps eyes moving quickly between terrain and map symbols.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Keeping the full map unfolded during a run helps beginners see the entire park and prevents them from losing their place.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position the compass baseplate edge on the map before rotating the capsule to align orienting lines?
Which map feature makes an effective catching feature behind a control versus an attack point in front of it?
What measurement confirms that a Scout's double-pace count is calibrated for both flat trails and steep uphill terrain?
Why is it dangerous to let Scouts practice taking magnetic bearings while leaning over a steel picnic table or belt buckle?
